objectives: State the three laws of motion in your own words.
Use F = ma to connect force, mass and acceleration.
Tell an action–reaction pair from a balanced pair of forces.
Estimate the acceleration of a cart from a measured force.

sections.body:
A body keeps its velocity unless a net force acts on it. That is the **first law**: inertia. The **second law** says the net force on a body equals the rate of change of its momentum; for a constant mass it shrinks to the famous F = ma. The **third law** says forces come in pairs: when body A pushes body B, body B pushes body A back with a force of the same size in the opposite direction.

Mass measures inertia: the more mass a body has, the harder it is to change its velocity. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass, and it changes with gravity while the mass does not.
sections.heading: Three laws in words

symbols.label: a

terms.gloss: A push or a pull, measured in newtons; a vector with size and direction.
The quantity of matter in a body, measured in kilograms; the source of inertia.
The rate of change of velocity, measured in metres per second squared.

sections.body:
The second law is a working tool. Measure the mass of the cart, measure the force you apply, and the acceleration comes out of one division. Double the force and the acceleration doubles; double the mass and the acceleration halves.

**Action and reaction never cancel each other**, because they act on different bodies. The horse pulls the cart forward; the cart pulls the horse backward. Whether the pair speeds up or not depends on the other forces on each body, not on the pair itself.
examples: A 2 kg cart feels a net force of 6 N. Its acceleration is a = F/m = 6/2 = 3 m/s².
A 1,000 kg car brakes from 20 m/s to rest in 4 s. The deceleration is 5 m/s², so the braking force is F = ma = 1,000 × 5 = 5,000 N.
sections.heading: F = ma at work
steps: Draw the body and every force that acts on it, with directions.
Add the forces as vectors to get the net force.
Write F = ma along each direction and solve for the unknown.
Check the units: newtons equal kilograms times metres per second squared.

rows: Velocity stays constant without a net force.
A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes.
Net force equals mass times acceleration.
A loaded trolley is harder to start.
Forces come in equal, opposite pairs.
A rocket pushes gas down; the gas pushes the rocket up.

item.summary: Three sentences carry the whole of classical mechanics: inertia, F = ma, and action with reaction. With them you can predict the motion of carts, rockets and planets.
item.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
